newsitem.title: USA: Ill. officials say toll road needed despite ruling.
newsitem.headline: Ill. officials say toll road needed despite ruling.

text.p: Illinois transportation officials said Friday they are optimistic they can demonstrate the importance of a planned expansion of a tollroad in the wake of a federal court ruling that put the brakes on the project.

Dave Loveday, spokesman for the Illinois State Toll Highway Authority, said both the authority and the state transportation department believe they can provide evidence of the importance of the tollroad expansion and why the project would not impact air quality.

U.S. District Court Judge Suzanne Conlon ruled Thursday that Illinois failed to evaluate alternatives to the toll road or the effect it would have on air quality. She directed transportation officials to produce studies justifying their conclusions or "explain why such critical studies are not possible."
The ruling stalled plans for a $700 million, bond-financed extension of I-355 south 12.5 miles from DuPage County into Will County in northeastern Illinois.

Bear, Stearns & Co. had been selected as senior manager for the bond deal planned for this spring. The tollway authority had been poised to award the first contracts for the project at its meeting later this month.

Julian D'Esposito, chairman of the tollway authority, said the agency "continues to be confident the road will be built ultimately." He said lawyers for the authority and the other defendants in the case, which include the U.S. and Illinois departments of transportation, need to confer on their next step.
D'Esposito said there were a lot of alternatives available including presenting more evidence to backup up conclusions for the toll road or appealing Conlon's ruling.
The ruling came in a lawsuit filed by environmental groups in August. That lawsuit claimed the environmental impact statement for the project was flawed.

A news release from the Chicago-based Environmental Law & Policy Center, which headed up the lawsuit, said the ruling would likely doom Illinois' plan to begin construction on the extension this spring.
"These agencies must now seriously study better alternatives to costly and environmentally destructive tollways," said Robert Michaels, staff attorney for the center.
Chuck Emrich, an analyst at Moody's Investors Service, said the rating agency would talk to tollway officials to assess the situation.
"We need to find out the extension of the impact and how they are going to address the situation," Emrich said.
The south extension of I-355 was the first leg of a $2.4 billion, 75-mile toll road extension approved by the Illinois General Assembly in 1993.
In August, Gov. Jim Edgar gave the green light to the 12.5-mile south extension, saying it would "aid the continued economic growth in the area."
